text.p: Joint venture talks between Britain's General Electric Co and Finmeccanica of Italy could create a partnership of huge potential that could speed up consolidation of Europe's defence industry, analysts said on Thursday.
GEC and Finmeccanica signed a memorandum of understanding in London this week to explore opportunities in defence collaboration.

The British group said the two would "study opportunities for future technological, manufacturing and commercial collaboration between their respective defence subsidiaries, Alenia Difesa and GEC-Marconi".
"They're a good fit," said one analyst. "Any defence deal which provides better economies of scale and a wider product range will reap benefits.
"It is also a step in the right direction and may trigger further European consolidation in the process."
Sash Tusa, a UBS analyst, said Finmeccanica was a good partner for GEC, which has flirted with the idea of merging with British rival British Aerospace for the past 12 years to no avail.
"Finmeccanica gets in effect the bulk of Italian defence spending and is a major company with clout. There's overlap in most of the core activities and they're already partners," said Tusa.
The Italian group accounts for 70 percent of the country's defence business and has defence sales of $1.39 billion.

The agreement to enter talks for the next few months was signed by Fabiano Fabiani, the Finmeccanica president, and GEC's managing director George Simpson, who has shaken the British corporate giant out of its strategic slumber since taking over from veteran chief Lord Weinstock.
Simpson made the move to start talks last November. The British group said in a statement that the two shared "a common vision of the evolution of the defence industry worldwide".
The U.S. defence industry is further ahead in a consolidation process and thus better able to compete in tough defence export markets.
"Finmeccanica and GEC recognise that the further consolidation of the European defence industry is necessary to ensure its continued efficiency and profitability," the statement said.

"We've already been involved with Alenia on a number of projects -- Tornado (fighter jets), the Eurofighter radar system and radar for Horizon frigates, for example," a spokesman for GEC-Marconi told Reuters.
He said these were already major programmes linking the two groups. "In total, what they do is very similar to our business right across the board," he added.
If the two defence arms link up, their combined business could total around one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) and encompass sectors like avionics, radar, missile seekers and torpedoes.

Some industry observers believe the two were brought together partly through frustrated efforts to forge links in the French defence industry, which is in stalemate as the government decides on the fate of Thomson-CSF -- the state defence electronics group.

France has taken a nationalist line and is opposed to a foreign firm taking control of Thomson-CSF -- a move which has led to companies looking elsewhere in Europe, analysts say. ($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
